# 3\. Results

## 3.1 Hypothesis 1

For each of the six dependent variables, we report estimates from Model 3, which offered the best balance between convergence diagnostics (Rhat \< 1.01, bulk ESS \> 1000\) and out-of-sample predictive performance (ELPD-LOO) among Models 1–3. Table X summarizes the key parameters from Model 3 across all six dependent variables, and Figure 1 shows posterior predictions of effort across correction phases by modality. Following a model-comparison rather than model-selection logic (McElreath, 2020), we additionally draw on Model 2 for correlations between random intercepts and slopes, and on Model 4 for pre-registered interactions; both are not estimated in Model 3 by design. Estimates of the primary effects remained stable across Models 1–4, indicating that our findings are robust to random effects specification. As expected, Model 0 showed notably larger correction-effect estimates, since with only the primary predictor in the model, correction absorbs variance that Models 1–4 partition into covariates and random slopes. Full outputs for all models are reported in the Supplementary Material; substantive between-model differences are flagged in the main text as they arise

**Figure 1\.** Posterior predictions of effort across correction phases by modality. Predicted effort is shown for the six dependent variables: cumulative measures (top row, integrals) and instantaneous measures (bottom row, peak means) of arm torque, amplitude envelope, and centre of pressure (COP). Distributions show posterior means with 89% (which line is it?) and 95% (which line is it?) highest density intervals (HDIs) from Model 3, with raw trial-level values overlaid as jittered points (log scale???). Dashed lines mark the baseline (c0) posterior mean for each modality as a reference. c0 \= baseline performance, c1 \= first correction, c2 \= second correction.

### 3.1.1 Cumulative effort

#### Arm torque change (integral)



c1 elicited 21.4% more effort (95% CrI: [15.5%, 27.4%];
β = 0.194, [0.144, 0.243])

Cumulative upper-limb effort reliably increased across both corrections. The first correction (c1) elicited 21.4% more effort than baseline (95% CrI: \[15.5%, 27.4%\]; from *baseline mean in real backtransformed units* to *c1 mean backtransformed* on average; β \= 0.194 on the log scale, \[0.144, 0.243\]), and the second correction (c2) elicited a further 15.7% more effort than the first (95% CrI: \[9.1%, 22.7%\]; from c1 backtransofrmed mean to c2 backtransformed mean; β \= 0.146 on the log scale, \[0.087, 0.205\]). In other words, when participants had to repair their original message, they produced more forceful gestures than at baseline and more forceful again on the second attempt, though the second escalation was smaller than the first. All estimates are averaged across modalities and reported at mean values of all continuous predictors.

Two predictors also showed credible effects on cumulative upper-limb effort: concept expressibility and modality. More expressible concepts required less effort: a 1 SD increase in expressibility predicted 8.4% less cumulative arm torque change (95% CrI: \[-14.8%, \-1.4%\]), averaged across modalities and at mean covariate values. Across the range of our stimulus set, this means that producing a low-expressibility concept (2 SD below the mean) required 41.7% more cumulative upper-limb effort than producing a high-expressibility concept (2 SD above the mean). Modality also mattered: participants invested \~16.6% more upper-limb effort in the gesture-only condition than in the multimodal condition (95% CrI: \[1.3%, 33.0%\]).  The modality effect did not vary across correction phases, as Model 4 showed no credible modality × correction interaction. Familiarity, extraversion, and trial number did not show credible effects.

Substantial variance in cumulative upper-limb effort was distributed across all three grouping levels. Concepts differed most in their baseline effort (SD \= 0.375 \[0.318, 0.441\], accounting for 25.7% total variance), followed by dyads (SD \= 0.318 \[0.228, 0.415\], 18.5%), and participants (SD \= 0.241 \[0.172, 0.318\], 10.6%). Beyond these baseline differences, participants varied in how strongly they responded to the first correction (SD \= 0.119 \[0.044, 0.179\]) and to modality (SD \= 0.246 \[0.194, 0.301\]), and concepts varied to a smaller extent in their sensitivity to modality (SD \= 0.149 \[0.090, 0.209\]). In Model 2, no correlations between random intercepts and slopes were credibly different from zero, indicating that participants who exerted more effort at baseline did not systematically differ in how they responded to corrections or modality. Notably, 44.5% of the total variance remained unexplained by the Model’s predictors and grouping structure, suggesting that additional sources of variation in upper-limb effort are not captured by our measured variables. 

#### Amplitude envelope (integral)

Cumulative vocal effort increased across both corrections. The first correction (c1) elicited an 11.8% increase compared to the baseline (95% CrI: \[7.8%, 16%\]; β \= \[backtransformed mean difference between c1 and c2\] or 0.112 on the log scale, \[0.075, 0.148\]), and the second correction (c2) elicited a further 7.7% increase over the first (95% CrI: \[3.5%, 12.0%\]; β \= 0.074 \[0.034, 0.114\]). In other words, when participants had to repair their original message, they produced louder vocalizations than at baseline and louder again on the second attempt, though the second escalation was smaller than the first.

Two predictors also showed credible effects on cumulative vocal effort: concept expressibility and modality. More expressible concepts required less effort: a 1 SD increase in expressibility predicted 8.4% less effort (95% CrI: \[-13.1%, \-3.5%\]), averaged across modalities and at mean covariate values. Across the range of our stimulus set, this translates to 42% difference between low-expressibility concepts (2 SD below the mean) and high-expressibility concepts (2 SD above the mean). Second, modality was also meaningful, with participants investing 38.6% more vocal effort in the vocal-only condition than in the multimodal condition (95% CrI: \[22.2%, 56.8%\]) – when participants could not use gestures alongside vocalizations, they relied more heavily on vocal effort to convey meaning. Familiarity, extraversion, and trial number did not show credible effects.

Model 4 (identical to Model 3 but with interactions) revealed a small but credible interaction between familiarity and correction, with effects in opposite directions across two corrections. Familiar dyads showed a larger increase in vocal effort at the first correction (c0→c1: \+4.2%, 95% CrI \[+x.x%, \+x.x%\]; β \= 0.041 on the log scale \[0.005, 0.077\]), but a smaller increase at the second correction (c1→c2: \-4.8%, 95% CrI \[-x.x%, \-x.x%\]; β \= \-0.049 \[-0.089, \-0.009\]). Importantly, the negative coefficient at the second correction reflects a reduction in the size of the increase rather than a reversal: familiar dyads still produce more vocal effort at the second correction than at the first, just less so than non-familiar dyads. This pattern suggests that familiar dyads may invest more vocal effort early in the repair sequence and de-escalate sooner across attempts, perhaps because they expect to resolve misunderstandings faster.

The largest contribution to variance in cumulative vocal effort came from participants, who differed substantially in their baseline vocal effort (SD \= 0.332 \[0.271, 0.401\], 28.8% of total variance). Concepts contributed a smaller but still substantial portion (SD \= 0.282 \[0.24, 0.331\], 20.2%), while dyad-level variance was both smaller and more uncertain (SD \= 0.165 \[0.018, 0.289\], 7.6%). Random slopes indicated that participants varied in their sensitivity to expressibility (SD \= 0.117 \[0.091, 0.145\]) and to modality (SD \= 0.205 \[0.163, 0.25\]), and concepts varied in their sensitivity to modality (SD \= 0.181 \[0.138, 0.229\]). Importantly, Model 2 revealed a credible negative correlation between participant-level baseline effort and expressibility sensitivity (r \= \-0.32, 95% CrI \[-0.55, \-0.07\]): participants who exerted more vocal effort overall showed smaller modulation of effort by concept expressibility. No other correlations between random intercepts and slopes reached credibility. Taken together, however, 43.1% of the total variance in cumulative vocal effort remains unexplained by the model’s predictors and grouping structure, suggesting that further sources of variation are not captured by the variables.

#### Change in center of pressure (integral)

Cumulative postural effort, measured as the integral of center of pressure (COP) change across the trial, increased reliably across both corrections. The first correction (c1) elicited a 12.6% increase relative to the baseline (95% CrI: \[8.3%, 17%\]; β \= add back-transformed), and the second correction (c2) elicited a further 11% increase over the first (95% CrI: \[6.3%, 16%\]; β \= add back-transformed). In contrast to the amplitude envelope finding, the magnitude of the increase remained approximately stable across two corrections, indicating that postural effort continued to increase at a similar rate rather than decelerating as repair progressed. All estimates are averaged across modalities and reported at mean values of all continuous predictors.

Two further predictors showed reliable effects on cumulative postural effort: extraversion and modality. More extroverted participants engaged in more cumulative postural effort: a 1-SD increase in extraversion predicted 10.5% more COP change (95% CrI: \[2.5%, 19.2%\]). Across the range of our sample, this means that a highly introverted person (2 SD below the mean) engaged in \~32.9% less cumulative postural effort than a highly extroverted person (2 SD above the mean). Modality had a particularly strong effect: direct contrasts confirm that conditions involving bodily movement elicited substantially more postural effort than the vocal-only condition (gesture-only vs. vocal-only: \~336.7% more; multimodal vs. vocal-only: \~349.2%), while the gesture-only and multimodal conditions did not differ credibly from each other. This pattern reflects the simple fact that posture-related effort is recruited primarily when the body is engaged in producing meaning. Familiarity, extraversion, and trial number did not show credible effects. 

Model 4 additionally showed a small but credible negative interaction between familiarity and the second correction (c1→c2: \-4.8% relative to the average correction effect \[95% CrI: \]; β \= \-0.049 \[-0.091, \-0.007\]). As with the envelope finding, the negative coefficient reflects the reduction in the size of the increase rather than a reversal: familiar dyads still showed more cumulative postural effort in the second correction compared to the first correction, but their escalation was attenuated relative to non-familiar dyads..  This pattern echoes the vocal-effort interaction in suggesting that familiar dyads may reach a plateau sooner across repair attempts.

The contribution to variance in cumulative postural effort was equally distributed between concepts (SD \= 0.378 \[0.323, 0.444\], 23.5% of total variance), dyads (SD \= 0.326 \[0.211, 0.439\], 17.7%), and participants (SD \= 0.315 \[0.253, 0.388\], 16.2%). Random slopes indicated that participants varied substantially in their sensitivity to modality (gesture-only: SD \= 0.329 \[0.268, 0.396\]; multimodal: SD \= 0.364 \[0.303, 0.432\]), and concepts varied to a smaller extent (gesture-only: SD \= 0.265 \[0.203, 0.335\]; multimodal: SD \= 0.200 \[0.136, 0.268\]). Importantly, Model 2 revealed credible positive correlations between concept-level baseline effort and modality sensitivity (gesture-only: r \= 0.494 \[95% CrI: 0.251, 0.699\]; multimodal: r \= 0.319 \[95% CrI: 0.046, 0.563\]), indicating that concepts associated with more postural effort overall also showed larger modality-driven differences in postural effort. No other correlations between random intercepts and slopes reached credibility. (Residual missing)

Taken together, the three cumulative measures consistently support H1 for cumulative effort: arm torque, amplitude envelope, and COP change all increased reliably from baseline to the first correction (between 11.8% and 21.4%) and from the first to the second correction (between 7.7% and 15.7%). The increase was largest for upper-limb effort, indicating that arms are the most flexibly recruited modality during repair, while postural effort showed the most stable pattern of escalation across attempts. The consistency of these increases across three independent measures of bodily effort indicates that repair imposes a substantive physical cost on speakers, supporting the hypothesis that misunderstanding is resolved through increased effort investment rather than mere repetition.

### 3.1.2 Instantaneous effort

#### Arm torque change (peak mean)

None of the predictors showed reliable effects on instantaneous upper-limb effort. Neither the correction phase nor any of the covariates (modality, expressibility, familiarity, extraversion, trial number) produced effects whose 95% credible intervals excluded zero. This null finding is itself informative: while cumulative upper-limb effort increased substantially across corrections (Section 3.1.1 above), the *peak* magnitude of torque change per movement event remained stable.

Variance was distributed between participants (SD \= 0.135 \[0.1, 0.171\], 10.7% of total variance) and concepts (SD \= 0.117 \[0.093, 0.144\], 8.0%), though to a lesser extent than for cumulative measures.  Participants also varied in modality sensitivity (gesture: SD \= 0.135 \[0.094, 0.176\]), but baseline effort did not correlate credibly with modality sensitivity in Model 2\. Crucially, 77.5% of the total variance in instantaneous upper-limb effort remains unexplained by the model’s predictors and grouping structure, the largest residual share of any measure we examined.

#### Amplitude envelope (peak mean)

Instantaneous vocal effort showed a small but reliable *decrease* in the first correction, but not in the second. Compared to baseline, peak vocal effort decreased by 4.9% at the first correction (95% CrI: \[-8.9%, \-0.7%\]); from **backtransf to backtransform** on average; β \= \-0.05 on the log scale, \[-0.093, \-0.007\]). The second correction showed no further credible change. In other words, when participants repaired their original message for the first time, they produced quieter vocalizations than at baseline. This pattern – a small decrease at c1 with no continued change at c2 – runs counter to H1 and contrasts with the cumulative envelope findings (Section 3.1.1): although participants produced more *total* vocal effort during repair, the *peak* loudness of their vocalizations did not increase. 

Two predictors showed reliable effects on instantaneous vocal effort: expressibility and modality. More expressible concepts were associated with less peak vocal effort: a 1 SD increase in expressibility predicted 6.6% less peak envelope (95% CrI: \[-12.2%, \-0.5%\]). Across the range of our stimulus set, this means that producing a low-expressibility concept (2 SD below the mean) required 31.5% more peak vocal effort than producing a high-expressibility concept (2 SD above the mean). In terms of modality, participants invested \~27.8% more peak vocal effort in the vocal-only condition than in the multimodal condition (CrI) – when participants could not use gesture, their peak vocal magnitude was higher. Familiarity, extraversion, and trial number did not show credible effects. 

Model 4 additionally showed a small but credible positive interaction between familiarity and the first correction (c0→c1: 6.7% relative to the average correction effect \[95% CrI: \];  β \= back-transformed). The positive coefficient indicates that familiar dyads showed less of a decrease in peak vocal effort at the first correction than non-familiar dyads. This pattern suggests that familiar dyads may not down-regulate peak vocal effort as steeply during early repair, perhaps because they are more open to maintaining effort levels with someone they know.

Variance in peak vocal effort was distributed across all three grouping levels, with the largest contribution from concepts (SD \= 0.390 \[0.331, 0.458\], 32.8% of total variance), followed by participants (SD \= 0.226 \[0.177, 0.282\], 11%). Random slopes also revealed that participants varied in their sensitivity to expressibility of concepts (SD \= 0.126 \[0.093, 0.16\]) and modality (vocal-only: SD \= 0.208 \[0.154, 0.264\]), and concepts varied in their sensitivity to modality (vocal-only: SD \= 0.199 \[0.147, 0.257\]). No correlations between random intercepts and slopes reached credibility in Model 2\. Notably, 51.5% of the total variance remained unexplained by the model.

#### Change in center of pressure (peak mean)

Instantaneous postural effort reliably decreased in the first correction, but not in the second. Compared to baseline,  peak COP change decreased by 3.1% at the first correction (95% CrI: \[-5.8%, \-0.2%\]; β \= add backtransformed); the second correction showed no further credible change. This means that participants produced movement that elicited smaller postural adjustments in terms of the average amplitude peak when correcting their performance for the first time. As with the envelope finding above, this pattern runs counter to H1 for instantaneous effort and contrasts with the cumulative postural finding: though *total* postural effort increased during repair, the average *peak* of postural shifts decreased slightly.

Two predictors also showed credible effects on instantaneous postural effort: extraversion and modality. More extroverted participants showed greater peak COP change: a 1-SD increase in extraversion was associated with \~7.1% higher peak postural effort (95% CrI: \[2%, 12.3%\]). Across our sample, this means that a highly introverted person (2 SD below the mean) engaged in \~24% less effort than a highly extroverted person (2 SD above the mean). Modality had a strong effect, similar in pattern to the cumulative finding. Direct contrasts revealed substantial differences between conditions involving bodily movement and the vocal condition (gesture-only vs. vocal-only: \~129.6%; multimodal vs. vocal-only: \~160.9%), and the multimodal condition elicited \~12.1% more peak postural effort than gesture-only. The fact that multimodal exceeds gesture-only here, despite producing similar cumulative effort, suggests that combining modalities recruits bursts of postural effort even though it does not increase total postural adaptation. Familiarity and trial number did not show credible effects. 

Model 4 additionally revealed a small but credible positive interaction between multimodal condition and expressibility (10.2% \[95% CrI: \]; β \= 0.097 \[0.021, 0.173\]), suggesting that more expressible concepts drove more instantaneous postural effort specifically in the multimodal condition. This pattern suggests that the multimodal condition may amplify expressibility-driven differences in the use of postural peaks, perhaps because participants more readily produce decisive, high-magnitude movements when they have multiple modalities to coordinate.

Variance was distributed across concepts and participants, with smaller dyad-level contributions. Concepts differed most in their baseline postural effort (SD \= 0.286 \[0.244, 0.336\], 28.8% of total variance), followed by participants (SD \= 0.218 \[0.177, 0.264\], 16.8%); dyad-level variance was small but present (SD \= 0.132 \[0.026, 0.217\]). Random slopes showed that participants also varied in their sensitivity to modality (gesture-only: SD \= 0.239 \[0.196, 0.287\]; multimodal: SD \= 0.204 \[0.162, 0.249\]), and concepts varied to a lesser extent (gesture-only: SD \= 0.154 \[0.107, 0.203\]; multimodal: SD \= 0.181 \[0.135, 0.231\]). Importantly, Model 2 showed credible positive correlations between concept-level baseline effort and modality sensitivity (gesture-only: r \= 0.640 \[95% CrI: 0.396, 0.832\]; multimodal: r \= 0.614 \[95% CrI: 0.406, 0.781\]), indicating that concepts associated with more peak postural effort also showed larger modality-driven differences. No other correlations between random intercepts and slopes reached credibility. Around 50.2% of the total variance remained unexplained by the model’s parameters.

Taken together, the three instantaneous measures present a strikingly different picture from the cumulative ones. While cumulative effort increased reliably across corrections for all three measures (Section 3.1.1), instantaneous effort either showed *no change* (arm torque) or a *small decrease* (envelope and COP) at the first correction. This dissociation does not support H1 for instantaneous effort: although repair imposes a clear cumulative cost on speakers, it does not appear to recruit greater peak intensity per movement or per vocalization. Instead, the pattern is consistent with a redistribution of effort across more time and more movement units rather than a concentrated scaling-up of force or amplitude \- we explore this further in the Discussion.

## 3.2 Hypothesis 2

H2 predicted that a higher degree of misunderstanding would require a performer to engage in more effortful correction. We operationalized the degree of misunderstanding as the cosine similarity between the guesser’s previous answer and the target meaning (lower similarity \= more misunderstanding), and tested this prediction across six dependent variables (like H1, Section 3.1). 

The data partially support H2: the effect of cosine similarity on effort is restricted to the upper-limb measures. Both cumulative and instantaneous upper-limb effort decreased credibly as the previous answer became more similar to the target. For each 1-SD increase in cosine similarity, cumulative upper-limb effort decreased by \~7.6% (95% CrI: \[-10.8%, \-4.1%\]; β \= backtr delta) and instantaneous upper-limb effort decreased by \~3.2% (95% CrI: \[-5.7%, \-0.9%\]; β \= backtr delta). In other words, when the guesser’s previous answer was closer to the target – that is, when there was less misunderstanding to repair – performers invested less arm effort in their next attempt.

However, neither cumulative nor instantaneous vocal effort showed a credible relationship with cosine similarity, and the same was true for both postural measures (see Figure 2). Vocal and postural effort thus appear to be insensitive to the degree of misunderstanding the performer is responding to, whereas arm movement adapts reliably to the amount of repair work the previous answer requires. Importantly, the upper-limb cosine similarity effect was uniformly distributed across the sample: variance in random slopes for cosine similarity was negligible across all three grouping levels (concepts, participants, and dyads), indicating that the effect did not vary systematically by performer, dyad, or concept. This consistency suggests that arm movement responds to common ground in a relatively automatic way, rather than reflecting strategic adaptation by particular individuals or for particular concepts. ## 3.3 Exploratory analysis

### 3.3.1 Time as covariate

Additional models for cumulative dependent variables with trial duration as a predictor revealed substantial attenuation of the main effect of correction on the effort. The effect of first correction (c0 → c1) on the upper-limb effort remains credibly positive, but decreased from 21.4 % to 7.2%, suggesting that two thirds of the increase can be attributed to longer duration but not necessarily bigger amplitude. Second correction (c1 → c2) of upper-limb effort and both corrections for vocal and postural effort are purely driven by duration, as neither of the predictors is now reliably different from zero. Additionally, expressibility and modality effect for upper-limb effort, too, can be attributed to duration, as both predictors do not yield credible estimates.

### 3.3.2 Baseline trial effort

A model with interaction between correction and baseline (c0) effort further enlightens the relationship between effort and correction. The main effect for cumulative upper-limb, vocal and postural effort remains essentially unchanged and is credibly positive. Unlike in models fitted to H1, first correction (c0 → c1) now yields a small but credible effect on instantaneous upper-limb effort by an increase of \~4% (CrI:), that is with a first trial at the grand mean. The effect of correction on instantaneous vocal effort is not credible anymore, and the effect on instantaneous postural effort remains essentially unaltered (i.e., small decrease). Second correction remains similar to models for H1, positively scaled with cumulative but not instantaneous effort for all three variables. Crucially, there is a negative interaction between the first correction (c0 → c1) and the first trial effort for all six DVs, indicating that increase in the effort at the baseline performance leads to attenuation of the increase at following correction. More specifically, first trials that are characterized by 2 SD more effort than the average are followed by a decrease in effort, while first trials that are characterized by 2 SD less effort than the average are followed by an increase.

### 3.3.3 Communicative gain

#### Does effort helps resolve trials at first attempt (and does it differ per modality)?

Predicted P(resolved) at the mean cumulative upper-limb effort level was 0.29 \[0.10, 0.59\] for gesture-only and 0.46 \[0.37, 0.56\] for multimodal trials. Predicted P(resolved) at the mean cumulative vocal effort level was 0.17 \[0.06, 0.40\] for vocal-only trials and 0.46 \[0.37, 0.56\] for multimodal. Predicted P(resolved) at the mean cumulative postural effort level was 0.29 \[0.10, 0.59\] for gesture-only, 0.17 \[0.06, 0.40\] for vocal only, and 0.46 \[0.37, 0.56\] for multimodal trials. These differences likely reflect the overall modality difference in baseline resolution probability. 

Effort productivity – defined as the change in P(resolved) between \-1 SD and \+1 SD effort – was small, ranging from \-0.14 to \+0.14 . The largest productivity values were observed for cumulative upper-limb effort in gesture-only trials (ΔP \= \+0.14) and for cumulative vocal effort in vocal-only trials (X). **However, none of these differences were accompanied by credible slopes across any feature and modality combination, indicating that physical effort did not reliably predict whether a concept was successfully communicated, and this did not differ across uni- or multimodal trials.**

Predicted P(resolved) at the mean instantenous upper-limb effort level was 0.281 \[0.059, 0.713\]  
 for gesture-only and 0.444 \[0.341, 0.549\] for multimodal trials. Predicted P(resolved) at the mean instantenous vocal effort level was 0.333 \[0.100, 0.688\] for vocal-only trials and 0.444 \[0.341, 0.549\] for multimodal. Predicted P(resolved) at the mean instantenous postural effort level was 0.281 \[0.059, 0.713\] for gesture-only, 0.333 \[0.100, 0.688\] for vocal only, and 0.281 \[0.059, 0.713\] for multimodal trials. 

Effort productivity showed diverging patterns from cumulative effort. **The largest productivity was observed for instantaneous vocal effort in vocal-only trials (ΔP \= \+0.32), indicating that higher intensity peaks were associated with higher probability of a trial being guessed on first attempt. This is also confirmed by a credible positive slope for envelope x vocal (b \= \+0.59 \[+0.12, \+1.07\]).** On the contrary, larger peaks in torque change were associated with smaller probability of guessing the meaning on the first attempt, but this difference was not accompanied by credible slope.

#### Does effort help guess the meaning faster (and does it differ per modality)?

To examine whether first-attempt cumulative effort predicted how quickly dyads eventually resolved a concept, we modelled ordinal resolution speed (c0 \> c1 \> c2 \> never resolved) as a function of effort measured exclusively at the first attempt, interacted with modality across three channels. At average first-attempt cumulative effort, modality was the dominant predictor of resolution speed: multimodal trials had the highest probability of first-attempt resolution (P(c0) \= 0.42), followed by gesture (P(c0) \= 0.30) and vocal trials (P(c0) \= 0.15), with the probability of never resolving highest in vocal trials (P(never) \= 0.48) and lowest in multimodal (P(never) \= 0.19). Note that the difference between gesture-only and multimodal trials was not credible, indicated by wide credible interval that includes zero.

No effort × modality interaction was credible at the 95% level for any channel, and the fixed effects for arm torque (b \= 0.08 \[−0.16, 0.32\]) and vocal envelope (b \= 0.15 \[−0.13, 0.43\]) did not credibly differ from zero. This indicates that, controlling for modality and concept expressibility, how much cumulative effort a speaker invested on their first attempt did not reliably predict whether the concept was eventually resolved quickly or slowly.

Productivity gradients — the change in P(c0) between −1 SD and \+1 SD of first-attempt effort — were small across all channels and modalities (range: −0.12 to \+0.15). The only numerically notable trend was a positive gradient for arm torque in gesture-only trials (ΔP(c0) \= \+0.15; ΔP(never) \= −0.15), suggesting that more cumulative gestural effort at first attempt was weakly associated with higher probability of immediate resolution and lower probability of never resolving. However, this trend was not credible and should be interpreted cautiously. All remaining gradients were negligible in magnitude and inconsistent in direction across modalities, providing no evidence that first-attempt cumulative effort in vocal or postural channels systematically predicts resolution trajectory.

To examine whether the instantaneous peak effort at first attempt predicted resolution trajectory, we fitted the same ordinal model using instantaneous rather than cumulative effort features. At average effort, multimodal trials showed the highest predicted probability of first-attempt resolution (P(c0) \= 0.42), followed by vocal (P(c0) \= 0.22) and gesture trials (P(c0) \= 0.20), with P(never) lowest in multimodal (0.19) and higher in gesture (0.40) and vocal (0.37). However, the modality contrasts did not reach credibility in this model (modality1: b \= 1.07 \[−0.46, 2.58\]; modality3: b \= 0.94 \[−0.23, 2.11\]), likely reflecting the smaller sample size relative to the full dataset (N \= 1,401 vs 2,548), and the predicted differences should be treated as non-credible trends rather than established effects. The overall direction of the modality pattern is consistent with the cumulative and c0 models where modality effects were credible. 

Unlike the cumulative model, one interaction reached credibility: instantaneous vocal envelope interacted with vocal modality (b \= −0.52 \[−0.91, −0.14\]), indicating that higher peak vocal amplitude at first attempt was associated with faster resolution specifically in vocal-only trials. This was reflected in the productivity gradients: envelope effort in vocal trials showed ΔP(c0) \= \+0.15 and ΔP(never) \= −0.20, meaning that dyads producing louder vocalisations on their first attempt were more likely to resolve immediately and substantially less likely to never resolve. This is the clearest evidence across all three resolution models of a prospective investment benefit, and its channel specificity — emerging in vocal trials for a vocal effort measure — is consistent with an interpretation of peak amplitude as a functionally relevant signal rather than a general arousal marker.

No other interaction was credible. Arm torque showed a small positive trend in gesture trials (ΔP(c0) \= \+0.08; ΔP(never) \= −0.12), consistent in direction with the cumulative model but not credible. COP showed small positive gradients across all modalities (all ΔP(c0) ≤ \+0.09) without any credible effects. The fixed effects for all three channels did not credibly differ from zero (arm torque: b \= 0.03 \[−0.35, 0.40\]; envelope: b \= 0.17 \[−0.09, 0.42\]; COP: b \= −0.12 \[−0.43, 0.19\]), indicating no reliable main effect of instantaneous effort on resolution speed averaging across modalities.

#### Does first-attempt effort predict whether a concept is ever resolved?

To address whether first-attempt effort predicted eventual communicative success — irrespective of how many corrections were needed — we fitted two binary logistic models predicting P(ever resolved), using cumulative (e4.m7_att) and instantaneous peak effort (e4.m7b_att) as predictors, both measured at the first attempt only.

At average effort, P(ever resolved) was highest in multimodal trials (cumulative: 0.83; instantaneous: 0.82), followed by gesture (cumulative: 0.70; instantaneous: 0.79) and vocal trials (cumulative: 0.53; instantaneous: 0.57). These modality differences reflect the structural advantage of richer communicative channels and replicated consistently across both operationalisations.

No effort × modality slope was credible in the cumulative model. Productivity gradients were modest and inconsistent in direction: the largest were observed for envelope in vocal trials (ΔP \= −0.24), envelope in multimodal trials (ΔP \= −0.18), and arm torque in vocal trials (ΔP \= \+0.22), but all CIs crossed zero. COP showed small positive trends across all modalities (ΔP range: \+0.05 to \+0.13). The absence of any credible effect in the cumulative model is consistent with the ordinal results reported earlier and suggests that cumulative first-attempt effort does not reliably predict whether a concept is eventually resolved.

The instantaneous model yielded two credible effects. First, envelope effort in multimodal trials showed a credible negative slope (b \= −0.36 \[−0.71, −0.03\]), with higher peak vocal amplitude at first attempt associated with lower P(ever resolved) in multimodal trials (ΔP \= −0.13; from P \= 0.88 at −1 SD to P \= 0.75 at \+1 SD). This pattern is consistent with louder vocalisation in multimodal trials marking communicative difficulty — when gesture is available but the speaker still raises their voice, the concept may be particularly hard to convey. Second, COP effort in vocal trials showed a credible positive slope (b \= \+0.69 \[+0.22, \+1.17\]), with higher peak postural displacement at first attempt associated with higher P(ever resolved) in vocal-only trials (ΔP \= \+0.21; from P \= 0.46 at −1 SD to P \= 0.67 at \+1 SD). This is the strongest prospective investment signal across all models: greater postural engagement at the moment of first articulation predicts eventual resolution in vocal trials, suggesting that postural effort may index speaker commitment or preparation in a way that carries communicative consequence even when gesture is not an available channel.

All remaining slopes were not credible. Arm torque showed positive but non-credible trends in gesture (ΔP \= \+0.19) and vocal trials (ΔP \= \+0.22), consistent in direction with the ordinal results but without sufficient precision to draw conclusions.
